title: Glossary
description: Terms used across these docs — discrete choice methods, the quantities they estimate, and the vocabulary of an experiment.

terms.definition: The average causal effect of changing one attribute from a baseline level to another level, holding the distribution of every other attribute fixed by the randomization. Reported with a confidence interval. This is the headline quantity a conjoint experiment estimates.

An experimental method that shows respondents profiles built from randomly assigned attribute levels and records which they choose. Because the levels are randomized, differences in choice rates identify causal effects rather than correlations.
An experiment in which each respondent picks one option from a set of competing alternatives. Modelling those picks recovers the trade-offs respondents make between attributes.

The framework underneath discrete choice: each alternative carries a utility made of a systematic part explained by its attributes and a random part, and the respondent picks the alternative with the highest total. Different assumptions about the random part produce different models.

The conditional logit model introduced by Daniel McFadden, in which the random part of utility is i.i.d. extreme value. Choice probabilities take a closed form, which makes it fast to estimate — at the cost of assuming every respondent shares the same preferences and of imposing IIA.

A choice model that lets preference coefficients vary across respondents by drawing them from a distribution, instead of forcing one shared coefficient. It captures preference heterogeneity and relaxes IIA.

terms.abbreviation: Integrated Choice and Latent Variable model
terms.definition: A choice model that treats unobserved constructs — attitudes, perceptions, motivations — as latent variables estimated jointly with the choice equation, rather than as raw survey answers plugged in as covariates.

The property that the odds of choosing between two alternatives do not depend on which other alternatives are available. Conditional logit imposes it; mixed logit does not. When it fails, adding a similar alternative draws share disproportionately from its near-twin.
One dimension of an alternative that the experiment varies — price, delivery time, brand, warranty. Attributes are the things whose causal effects the experiment measures.
One of the specific values an attribute can take. An attribute of price might have the levels $9, $19 and $29. Effects are always reported relative to a baseline level.
One complete alternative shown to a respondent — a full set of attributes, each fixed at one randomly assigned level.
A single screen presenting competing profiles from which the respondent picks one. A respondent normally completes several choice tasks, each with freshly randomized levels.
One simulated participant who completes the choice tasks. Respondents carry demographic and attitudinal characteristics, so effects can be estimated for the whole population or for a segment of it.
The set of simulated respondents an experiment runs on, constructed to match a target population's characteristics. It is what makes an experiment runnable before a product, price or message exists.
A published study with human respondents that an experiment is replicated against, so the synthetic result can be compared to a known human result rather than assessed on its own.

Re-running a published study's design on a synthetic population and comparing the estimated effects to the original human estimates. It is the evidence that a method transfers, not an assertion that it does.

The range of values consistent with the data at a stated confidence level. An estimate without one says nothing about how much of the number is noise, which is why every effect in these docs ships with one.

The change in an outcome produced by changing one input, with everything else held fixed by design. Randomizing attribute levels is what licenses the causal reading; observing a correlation in existing data does not.

The price change that exactly offsets the utility gain from some other attribute change — read off the ratio of that attribute's coefficient to the price coefficient. It converts an effect into money.
The estimated utility contribution of a single attribute level. Part-worths are the raw model coefficients that effects such as AMCE and willingness to pay are computed from.
